title: Ἵπποι δακρύοντες
about: The fight over Patroclus’ body is likened to men stretching an oxhide, and Achilles, far away, does not yet know that Patroclus is dead. Achaeans and Trojans each urge their side on to keep the body or to win it. Achilles’ immortal horses stand weeping beside the chariot and will not move, whatever Automedon does; Zeus pities them, puts strength into them, and they carry Automedon back into the fighting. Alone in the chariot he can drive but not fight, and when Alcimedon finds him and rebukes him, he hands over the reins and steps down to fight.

sentences.t:
τοῖς δὲ πανημερίοις ἔριδος μέγα νεῖκος ὀρώρει
ἀργαλέης· καμάτῳ δὲ καὶ ἱδρῷ νωλεμὲς αἰεὶ
γούνατά τε κνῆμαί τε πόδες θ’ ὑπένερθεν ἑκάστου
χεῖρές τ’ ὀφθαλμοί τε παλάσσετο μαρναμένοιιν
ἀμφ’ ἀγαθὸν θεράποντα ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο.
sentences.l:
To them, all day long, a great quarrel of grievous strife had risen up;
and with toil and sweat, unceasingly, always,
the knees and the shins and the feet below of each man,
the hands and the eyes were being spattered, of the two fighting
about the good attendant of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus.
sentences.i: All day long a great quarrel of grievous strife had risen up among them; and with toil and sweat, without pause, ever, the knees and shins and feet below, the hands and the eyes, of each of the two who fought about the good attendant of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus, were spattered.
sentences.n: This is the fight over Patroclus’ body. Αἰακίδαο is the genitive of Αἰακίδης ‘descendant of Aeacus’, and Patroclus is the θεράπων ‘attendant’ (the table’s ‘good attendant’, 16.165). The verb παλάσσετο ‘was spattered’ is singular and stands after its five subjects (γούνατα, κνῆμαι, πόδες, χεῖρες, ὀφθαλμοί); ὑπένερθεν ‘below’ goes with the feet. ἑκάστου μαρναμένοιιν is a genitive with a dual participle, ‘of each of the two fighting’, that is, each pair of opposed fighters. ἔριδος ἀργαλέης is ‘of grievous strife’; πανημερίοις is a dative adjective agreeing with τοῖς, ‘lasting the whole day’, and ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρωρα, ‘had risen’. Line 388 is already published (iliad-100), and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ ταύροιο βοὸς μεγάλοιο βοείην
λαοῖσιν δώῃ τανύειν μεθύουσαν ἀλοιφῇ·
sentences.l:
And as when a man the hide of a great bull
to the people gives to stretch, soaked with fat;
sentences.i: And as when a man gives the people the hide of a great bull to stretch, soaked with fat;
sentences.n: A comparison begins here and runs to 393: the struggle over the corpse is like men stretching a hide. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ is ‘and as when’, ταύροιο βοός is ‘of a bull’ (βοῦς is an ox or cow, here a bull; the two words together mean ‘a bull’), βοείην is ‘hide’ (an ox-hide), and λαοῖσιν is ‘to the people’, the men who will do the work. δώῃ is an aorist subjunctive, ‘gives’, with the infinitive τανύειν ‘to stretch’; μεθύουσαν is the participle of μεθύω ‘be drunk’, used of a hide ‘soaked’, and ἀλοιφῇ is the dative ‘with fat’ (the oil worked into it).

sentences.t:
δεξάμενοι δ’ ἄρα τοί γε διαστάντες τανύουσι
κυκλόσ’, ἄφαρ δέ τε ἰκμὰς ἔβη, δύνει δέ τ’ ἀλοιφὴ
πολλῶν ἑλκόντων, τάνυται δέ τε πᾶσα διὰ πρό·
sentences.i: they take it and, standing apart in a ring, stretch it, and the moisture goes at once and the fat sinks in as many pull, and the whole hide is stretched through and through;
sentences.n: Still the comparison. τοί γε is ‘they’, the people who took the hide; δεξάμενοι is ‘having received’, an aorist middle participle, and διαστάντες ‘having stood apart’. κυκλόσε is ‘in a circle’ (the elided κυκλόσ’), and ἰκμάς is ‘moisture’. The three τε’s in ἄφαρ δέ τε, δύνει δέ τ’ and τάνυται δέ τε are the epic τε of a general scene, and the aorist ἔβη ‘goes’ is the timeless aorist of such a scene. πολλῶν ἑλκόντων is a genitive absolute ‘many pulling’; διὰ πρό is ‘right through’, the hide being stretched all through.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἵ γ’ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα νέκυν ὀλίγῃ ἐνὶ χώρῃ
εἵλκεον ἀμφότεροι· μάλα δέ σφισιν ἔλπετο θυμὸς
Τρωσὶν μὲν ἐρύειν προτὶ Ἴλιον, αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοῖς
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς·
sentences.l:
So they, hither and thither, the corpse in a small space
were dragging, both sides; and greatly for them hoped the heart,
for the Trojans to drag it to Ilios, but for the Achaeans
to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: So they dragged the corpse this way and that in a small space, both sides; and greatly did the Trojans’ hearts hope to drag it to Ilios, and the Achaeans’ to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: ὣς is the point of comparison: they pulled at the corpse as men pull the hide. οἵ γ’ is ‘they’, ἀμφότεροι ‘both sides’, and εἵλκεον is the imperfect of ἕλκω ‘drag’, with νέκυν ‘corpse’ and ὀλίγῃ ἐνὶ χώρῃ ‘in a small space’. θυμός is the ‘heart’, and σφισιν ‘for them’ is then split into Τρωσὶν μέν … Ἀχαιοῖς ‘for the Trojans … for the Achaeans’; ἔλπετο is ‘hoped’ (of what each side wanted), and ἐρύειν is ‘to drag’ (as ἐρύσαι at 419), with προτὶ Ἴλιον ‘to Ilios’ and νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς ‘to the hollow ships’.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ αὐτοῦ μῶλος ὀρώρει
ἄγριος·
sentences.l:
and about him the toil had risen
savage;
sentences.i: and about him the toil of battle had risen up, savage;
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ ‘him’ is the corpse, and μῶλος is the table’s ‘toil’ (μῶλος Ἄρηος, ‘toil of battle’), here the struggle. ἄγριος is the table’s ‘savage’; it stands first in the next line, set apart from its noun for emphasis. ὀρώρει is the same ‘had risen’ as in 384.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κ’ Ἄρης λαοσσόος οὐδέ κ’ Ἀθήνη
τόν γε ἰδοῦσ’ ὀνόσαιτ’, οὐδ’ εἰ μάλα μιν χόλος ἵκοι·
sentences.l:
and neither Ares, rouser of the people, nor Athena
seeing that one, would make light of it, not even if wrath came very much upon him;
sentences.i: and neither Ares, rouser of the people, nor Athena would make light of that struggle on seeing it, not even if wrath came very much upon him;
sentences.n: The sense is that the fight was so grim that even gods who delight in war would not scorn it. τόν γε is masculine and picks up μῶλος ‘that struggle’; ἰδοῦσ’ is ‘having seen’ (ἰδοῦσα, feminine, agreeing with Athena the nearer subject), and ὀνόσαιτ’ is the aorist optative of ὄνομαι ‘make light of’ (the table’s sense at 4.539; the other gloss, ‘find fault with’, is not taken). κ’ is κεν, and οὐδ’ εἰ is ‘not even if’. The pronoun μιν ‘him’ is singular where two gods are named, and the Greek does not say which of them is meant. λαοσσόος is the table’s ‘rouser of the people’, an epithet of Ares whose derivation is disputed (‘saving the people’ is also ancient).

sentences.t:
τοῖον Ζεὺς ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ ἀνδρῶν τε καὶ ἵππων
ἤματι τῷ ἐτάνυσσε κακὸν πόνον·
sentences.l:
Such an evil toil over Patroclus, of men and of horses,
Zeus on that day stretched out, an evil toil;
sentences.i: Such an evil toil of men and horses did Zeus stretch out over Patroclus on that day;
sentences.n: τοῖον … κακὸν πόνον is ‘such an evil toil’, the object of ἐτάνυσσε ‘stretched out’, with ἀνδρῶν τε καὶ ἵππων ‘of men and of horses’ going with πόνον; ἐτάνυσσε is the same verb as τανύειν and τάνυται in the comparison above, ‘stretch’, and the play on the stretched hide is the poet’s. ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ is ‘over Patroclus’, and ἤματι τῷ is ‘on that day’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ τι
ᾔδεε Πάτροκλον τεθνηότα δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l:
and not yet at all
knew Patroclus to be dead, heavenly Achilles;
sentences.i: But heavenly Achilles did not yet know at all that Patroclus was dead;
sentences.n: The poet turns to Achilles, who is away from the fight. οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ τι is ‘and not yet at all’, ᾔδεε is the pluperfect of οἶδα used as an imperfect, ‘knew’ (ᾔδεε in the epic form), and Πάτροκλον τεθνηότα is the accusative with a perfect participle, ‘Patroclus dead’, that is, ‘that Patroclus was dead’. δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the table’s ‘heavenly Achilles’.

sentences.t:
πολλὸν γὰρ ῥ’ ἀπάνευθε νεῶν μάρναντο θοάων
τείχει ὕπο Τρώων·
sentences.l:
for far apart from the swift ships they were fighting
beneath the wall of the Trojans;
sentences.i: for they were fighting far from the swift ships, under the wall of the Trojans;
sentences.n: Here the poet says why Achilles does not know. μάρναντο is ‘they were fighting’, the Achaeans round Patroclus; πολλὸν ἀπάνευθε is ‘far apart’ (the table’s ‘apart’), νεῶν θοάων is ‘the swift ships’, and τείχει ὕπο Τρώων is ‘beneath the wall of the Trojans’ (ὕπο is accented on the first syllable after its noun). γὰρ ῥ’ is γὰρ ῥα, ‘for indeed’.

sentences.t:
τό μιν οὔ ποτε ἔλπετο θυμῷ
τεθνάμεν, ἀλλὰ ζωὸν ἐνιχριμφθέντα πύλῃσιν
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ τὸ ἔλπετο πάμπαν
ἐκπέρσειν πτολίεθρον ἄνευ ἕθεν, οὐδὲ σὺν αὐτῷ·
sentences.l:
therefore never did he expect in his heart that he was dead,
but that, alive, having pressed hard up against the gates,
he would come back again, since not even this did he at all expect
to sack the citadel without himself, nor with him;
sentences.i: That is why he never expected in his heart that Patroclus was dead, but that, alive, after pressing hard up against the gates, he would come back again, since he did not at all expect him to sack the citadel without himself, nor with him either;
sentences.n: τό is the neuter ‘therefore, for that reason’, and μιν ‘him’ is Patroclus. ἔλπετο is ‘expected’ (the table’s ἔλπομαι ‘expect’, 9.40; ‘hope’ is kept for what is wished for, as at 395), with the infinitives τεθνάμεν ‘to be dead’ and ἀπονοστήσειν ‘would come back’ (a future infinitive); ζωόν ‘alive’ and ἐνιχριμφθέντα ‘having pressed hard up against’ (aorist passive of ἐγχρίμπτω, as at 7.272) agree with the unnamed Patroclus. In the second clause οὐδὲ τό is ‘nor this’, pointing ahead to ἐκπέρσειν, which the second ἔλπετο takes ‘to sack’ with πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’. ἄνευ ἕθεν is ‘without himself’ (ἕθεν the reflexive, Achilles); who σὺν αὐτῷ ‘with him’ is, Achilles or Patroclus, the Greek does not say, and the English keeps ‘him’.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι γὰρ τό γε μητρὸς ἐπεύθετο νόσφιν ἀκούων,
ἥ οἱ ἀπαγγέλλεσκε Διὸς μεγάλοιο νόημα.
sentences.l:
for often he learned that from his mother, hearing it apart,
who used to report to him the thought of great Zeus.
sentences.i: for he often learned this from his mother, hearing it in private, who used to report to him the thought of great Zeus.
sentences.n: The ‘that’ is that Troy would not fall to Patroclus. τό γε is ‘that indeed’, ἐπεύθετο ‘he learned’ (imperfect, with πολλάκι ‘often’), νόσφιν ‘apart’ (away from others), and ἀκούων ‘hearing’. ἥ is the relative ‘who’, Thetis, who is not named in this part; ἀπαγγέλλεσκε is an iterative imperfect ‘used to report’, and Διὸς μεγάλοιο is ‘of great Zeus’. νόημα is the table’s ‘thought’.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε γ’ οὔ οἱ ἔειπε κακὸν τόσον ὅσσον ἐτύχθη
μήτηρ, ὅττί ῥά οἱ πολὺ φίλτατος ὤλεθ’ ἑταῖρος.
sentences.l:
Then indeed not to him did she say an evil so great as had come about,
his mother, that to him by far the dearest companion had perished.
sentences.i: But then his mother did not tell him how great an evil had come about, that his companion, by far the dearest to him, had perished.
sentences.n: The mother is Thetis, and the ‘evil’ is the death of Patroclus. δὴ τότε γ’ is ‘then indeed’ (the Greek has no ‘but’; the English adds one to join the sentence to what goes before); οἱ is ‘to him’, and ἔειπε is ‘said’ (reduplicated aorist of εἶπον). κακὸν τόσον ὅσσον is ‘an evil so great as’, ἐτύχθη an aorist passive of τεύχω ‘was wrought, came about’, and ὅττι ‘that’ opens what she did not say; πολὺ φίλτατος ἑταῖρος is ‘by far the dearest companion’ and ὤλεθ’ is ὤλετο ‘perished’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ αἰεὶ περὶ νεκρὸν ἀκαχμένα δούρατ’ ἔχοντες
νωλεμὲς ἐγχρίμπτοντο καὶ ἀλλήλους ἐνάριζον·
sentences.l:
But they, always about the corpse, holding pointed spears,
unceasingly pressed close and were slaying one another;
sentences.i: But they, always holding pointed spears about the corpse, pressed close without pause and killed one another;
sentences.n: The fight round the body goes on. οἳ δ’ is ‘but they’; ἀκαχμένα is the perfect passive participle of the root of ἀκή ‘point’, the table’s ‘pointed’, agreeing with δούρατ’ ‘spears’. ἐγχρίμπτοντο is the middle of ἐγχρίμπτω ‘press close’, with νωλεμές (adverb) ‘unceasingly’, and ἐνάριζον is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω, which strictly is ‘strip a slain man’, but here the killing is the point and the table’s ‘killing’ is kept (9.530).

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων·
sentences.l: and thus someone used to say, of the bronze-shirted Achaeans:
sentences.i: And this is how one of the bronze-shirted Achaeans would speak:
sentences.n: A speech introduction: ὧδε is ‘thus’, τις ‘someone’, and εἴπεσκεν is an iterative imperfect, ‘used to say’, because many men said it in turn; the speaker is not one man. Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων is the table’s ‘bronze-shirted Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι οὐ μὰν ἧμιν ἐϋκλεὲς ἀπονέεσθαι
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς,
sentences.l:
“Friends, truly not for us is it of good fame to go back
to the hollow ships,
sentences.i: “Friends, it is no credit to us to go back to the hollow ships,
sentences.n: This is the speech of an unnamed Achaean. ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’; οὐ μάν is ‘truly not’, ἧμιν is the epic ἡμῖν ‘for us’, and ἐϋκλεές is ‘of good fame’ (εὖ and κλέος), which the English puts as ‘no credit’. ἀπονέεσθαι is the infinitive ‘to go back’, with νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς ‘to the hollow ships’ (ἔπι placed after its noun).
sentences.mark: An Achaean urges his fellows on

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ γαῖα μέλαινα
πᾶσι χάνοι·
sentences.l:
but here may the dark earth
gape for us all;
sentences.i: but may the dark earth gape open for us all, here;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ is ‘but’, in the sense ‘rather’; αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘here, on the spot’ (not the genitive of αὐτός). χάνοι is an aorist optative of χάσκω ‘gape’, a wish, and γαῖα μέλαινα is the table’s ‘the dark earth’; πᾶσι ‘for all’ means for all of them, the speaker and his fellows.

sentences.t:
τό κεν ἧμιν ἄφαρ πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη
εἰ τοῦτον Τρώεσσι μεθήσομεν ἱπποδάμοισιν
ἄστυ πότι σφέτερον ἐρύσαι καὶ κῦδος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.l:
that would at once be far better for us,
if this man to the Trojans, tamers of horses, we shall give up
to drag to their own city and win glory.”
sentences.i: that would be far better for us at once, if we are going to give this man up to the Trojans, tamers of horses, to drag to their own city and win glory.”
sentences.n: τό ‘that’ is the earth’s gaping in the clause before; κεν … εἴη is ‘would be’, with κέρδιον ‘better’ (the table’s comparative) and ἄφαρ ‘at once’. The εἰ-clause names the case in which that would be better: ‘if we are going to give him up’, with μεθήσομεν a future of μεθίημι ‘let go’ and τοῦτον ‘this man’ the corpse; Τρώεσσι … ἱπποδάμοισιν is the table’s ‘Trojans, tamers of horses’. ἐρύσαι is an aorist infinitive ‘to drag’ and κῦδος ἀρέσθαι ‘to win glory’ (the table’s ‘win’); ἄστυ πότι σφέτερον is ‘to their own city’ (πότι is πρός).

sentences.t: ὣς δέ τις αὖ Τρώων μεγαθύμων αὐδήσασκεν·
sentences.l: And so in turn someone of the great-hearted Trojans used to speak:
sentences.i: And in turn one of the great-hearted Trojans would speak:
sentences.n: The Trojan answer. αὖ is ‘in turn’, τις ‘someone’, and αὐδήσασκεν is an iterative aorist (-σκ-) of αὐδάω ‘speak’, ‘used to speak’, again of many speakers. Τρώων μεγαθύμων is the table’s ‘great-hearted Trojans’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, εἰ καὶ μοῖρα παρ’ ἀνέρι τῷδε δαμῆναι
πάντας ὁμῶς, μή πώ τις ἐρωείτω πολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
“Friends, even if it is fate beside this man to be overcome,
all alike, let no one yet hold back from war.”
sentences.i: “Friends, even if it is our fate to be overcome, all of us together, beside this man, let none of us yet hold back from the war.”
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is again ‘friends’. εἰ καὶ is ‘even if’ and μοῖρα is ‘fate’ (with ἐστί understood), with the infinitive δαμῆναι ‘to be overcome’, an aorist passive; παρ’ ἀνέρι τῷδε is ‘beside this man’, the corpse, and πάντας ὁμῶς is ‘all alike, all together’. μή πώ τις ἐρωείτω is a negative command in the third person, ‘let no one yet’, from ἐρωέω ‘hold back’, with πολέμοιο ‘from war’ as the table has it (13.776).

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τις εἴπεσκε, μένος δ’ ὄρσασκεν ἑκάστου.
sentences.l: So then someone used to speak, and used to rouse the might of each.
sentences.i: So one man or another would speak, and rouse every man’s might.
sentences.n: The closing line of the exchanges. ὣς ἄρα is ‘so then’, τις ‘someone’, and εἴπεσκε and ὄρσασκεν are both iterative (-σκ-) forms, ‘used to say’ and ‘used to rouse’, since many spoke. μένος is ‘might’ (the table’s word, 2.387), and ἑκάστου ‘of each’ is a possessive genitive, the strength belonging to each man.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν μάρναντο, σιδήρειος δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς
χάλκεον οὐρανὸν ἷκε δι’ αἰθέρος ἀτρυγέτοιο·
sentences.l:
So they fought, and an iron din
reached the bronze heaven through the unharvested upper air;
sentences.i: So they fought, and an iron din reached the bronze heaven through the air that yields no harvest;
sentences.n: σιδήρειος is ‘iron’ and ὀρυμαγδός is the table’s ‘din’; χάλκεον οὐρανόν is ‘the bronze heaven’, the sky pictured as of bronze, and ἷκε is the unaugmented past tense of ἵκω, ‘reached’. δι’ αἰθέρος is ‘through the upper air’ (αἰθήρ the bright air above the clouds). ἀτρυγέτοιο is the word the table renders ‘unharvested’ / ‘that yields no harvest’ of the sea (ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο); it is applied here to the air, and its meaning is not known for certain.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δ’ Αἰακίδαο μάχης ἀπάνευθεν ἐόντες
κλαῖον, ἐπεὶ δὴ πρῶτα πυθέσθην ἡνιόχοιο
ἐν κονίῃσι πεσόντος ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο.
sentences.l:
But the horses of the descendant of Aeacus, being apart from the battle,
were weeping, since first the two learned
of the charioteer fallen in the dust by man-slaying Hector.
sentences.i: But the horses of the descendant of Aeacus, standing apart from the battle, were weeping, ever since the two of them first learned that their charioteer had fallen in the dust at the hands of man-slaying Hector.
sentences.n: The horses are Achilles’ pair, Xanthus and Balius, who are not named here; Αἰακίδαο is again ‘of the descendant of Aeacus’, Achilles. ἐόντες is ‘being’, and μάχης ἀπάνευθεν is ‘apart from the battle’. ἐπεὶ δὴ πρῶτα is ‘ever since first’; πυθέσθην is a dual aorist of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’ (‘the two learned’), and its object is the genitive with participle, ἡνιόχοιο … πεσόντος ‘of the charioteer fallen’, the charioteer being Patroclus. ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο is ‘by man-slaying Hector’ (the table’s ἀνδροφόνος).

sentences.t:
ἦ μὰν Αὐτομέδων Διώρεος ἄλκιμος υἱὸς
πολλὰ μὲν ἂρ μάστιγι θοῇ ἐπεμαίετο θείνων,
πολλὰ δὲ μειλιχίοισι προσηύδα, πολλὰ δ’ ἀρειῇ·
sentences.i: Automedon, Diores’ sturdy son, often lashed at them with the swift whip, striking them, and often spoke to them with gentle words, and often with threats;
sentences.n: Automedon is Achilles’ charioteer, who has taken Patroclus’ place. ἦ μάν is ‘truly’, and Διώρεος ἄλκιμος υἱός is ‘Diores’ sturdy son’ (the table’s ἄλκιμος υἱός). ἐπεμαίετο is the imperfect of ἐπιμαίομαι ‘lay a hand on, reach at’, here with the whip, and θείνων is ‘striking’; μάστιγι θοῇ is ‘with a swift whip’. μειλιχίοισι is ‘with gentle’ (words understood, ἔπεσσι), and ἀρειῇ is ‘with a threat’, a rare word, ‘threat’ by the usual explanation; the three πολλά are ‘many times, often’ and the verb προσηύδα ‘spoke to’ serves both of the last two clauses.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ οὔτ’ ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας ἐπὶ πλατὺν Ἑλλήσποντον
ἠθελέτην ἰέναι οὔτ’ ἐς πόλεμον μετ’ Ἀχαιούς,
sentences.l:
but the two neither back to the ships, to the broad Hellespont,
were willing to go, nor into the war among the Achaeans,
sentences.i: but the two were willing neither to go back to the ships, to the broad Hellespont, nor into the war among the Achaeans,
sentences.n: τὼ is the two horses, and ἠθελέτην is a dual imperfect ‘were willing’, so that the verb carries the refusal. οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ is ‘neither … nor’, ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας is ‘back to the ships’, and πλατὺν Ἑλλήσποντον is the table’s ‘the broad Hellespont’; μετ’ Ἀχαιούς is ‘among the Achaeans’. The sentence goes on in 434 with ἀλλ’ ‘but’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὥς τε στήλη μένει ἔμπεδον, ἥ τ’ ἐπὶ τύμβῳ
ἀνέρος ἑστήκῃ τεθνηότος ἠὲ γυναικός,
sentences.l:
but as a pillar stays firm, which upon a tomb
stands of a man dead or of a woman,
sentences.i: but as a pillar stays steady that stands on the tomb of a man or a woman who has died,
sentences.n: A comparison. ὥς τε is ‘as’, στήλη ‘pillar’ and τύμβος ‘tomb’ are the table’s words, and ἔμπεδον is ‘firmly’ (adverb). ἥ τ’ is the relative ‘which’ with the epic τε, and ἑστήκῃ is a perfect subjunctive of ἵστημι, ‘stands’; τεθνηότος agrees with ἀνέρος and the English lets it cover both the man and the woman.

sentences.t:
ὣς μένον ἀσφαλέως περικαλλέα δίφρον ἔχοντες
οὔδει ἐνισκίμψαντε καρήατα·
sentences.l:
so they stayed securely, holding the very fair chariot,
having fixed their heads in the ground;
sentences.i: so the two stayed there securely, holding the very fair chariot, with their heads fixed to the ground;
sentences.n: ὣς μένον is the imperfect ‘so they stayed’ (μένον is a plural form, the dual would be μενέτην, but the subject τώ is the two horses), the point of the comparison. ἀσφαλέως is ‘securely’, περικαλλέα is the table’s ‘very fair’, and δίφρον ἔχοντες is ‘holding the chariot’, the two standing with it unmoved. ἐνισκίμψαντε is a dual aorist participle of ἐνισκίμπτω ‘fix in’, ‘having fixed (their heads) in the ground’ (the English says ‘to the ground’), with οὔδει ‘ground’ in the dative and καρήατα ‘heads’.

sentences.t:
δάκρυα δέ σφι
θερμὰ κατὰ βλεφάρων χαμάδις ῥέε μυρομένοισιν
ἡνιόχοιο πόθῳ·
sentences.i: and hot tears ran down from their eyelids to the ground as they wept in longing for their charioteer;
sentences.n: δάκρυα … θερμά is the table’s ‘hot tears’, and σφι is ‘for them’, the horses. κατὰ βλεφάρων is ‘down from the eyelids’, χαμάδις is ‘to the ground’, and ῥέε is the imperfect ‘flowed’ (an uncontracted ῥέε). μυρομένοισιν is a dative plural participle, ‘as they wept’ (‘for them weeping’), and ἡνιόχοιο πόθῳ is ‘in longing for the charioteer’, with πόθος ‘longing’.

sentences.t:
θαλερὴ δ’ ἐμιαίνετο χαίτη
ζεύγλης ἐξεριποῦσα παρὰ ζυγὸν ἀμφοτέρωθεν.
sentences.l:
and the abundant mane was soiled,
having fallen down from the yoke-loop beside the yoke on either side.
sentences.i: and the abundant mane was soiled, trailing down from the yoke-loop on either side of the yoke.
sentences.n: θαλερή is ‘abundant’ (the table’s θαλερὸν δάκρυον, here of a mane), and χαίτη ‘mane’. ἐμιαίνετο is ‘was soiled’, an imperfect passive of μιαίνω, and ἐξεριποῦσα is the second-aorist participle of ἐξερείπω ‘fall down out of’, nominative feminine, which the English gives as ‘trailing down from’. ζεύγλη is the loop or strap by which the yoke is fastened to the horse; the exact part of the harness is not certain. παρὰ ζυγόν is ‘beside the yoke’ and ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘on both sides’.

sentences.t:
μυρομένω δ’ ἄρα τώ γε ἰδὼν ἐλέησε Κρονίων,
κινήσας δὲ κάρη προτὶ ὃν μυθήσατο θυμόν·
sentences.l:
And, seeing those two weeping, pitied them the son of Cronus,
and, shaking his head, he spoke to his own heart:
sentences.i: And the son of Cronus, seeing the two of them weeping, pitied them, and shaking his head he spoke to his own heart:
sentences.n: The son of Cronus is Zeus (the table’s ‘the son of Cronus’ for Κρονίων). μυρομένω … τώ γε is a dual, ‘those two weeping’, the horses, with ἰδών ‘seeing’ and ἐλέησε ‘pitied’. Line 442 already stands in a published part of the Odyssey, ‘shaking his head he spoke to his own heart’: κινήσας is ‘having shaken’, κάρη ‘head’, and προτὶ ὃν … θυμόν ‘to his own heart’, ὅς being the possessive ‘his own’. He speaks in his own heart, but the words that follow are addressed to the horses.

sentences.t:
ἆ δειλώ, τί σφῶϊ δόμεν Πηλῆϊ ἄνακτι
θνητῷ, ὑμεῖς δ’ ἐστὸν ἀγήρω τ’ ἀθανάτω τε;
sentences.l:
“Oh, you two miserable ones, why did we give you two to lord Peleus,
a mortal, when you yourselves are ageless and immortal?
sentences.i: “Oh, you two miserable ones, why did we give you two to lord Peleus, a mortal, when you yourselves are ageless and immortal?
sentences.n: The speech is Zeus’s, to the horses; they were a gift of the gods to Peleus, who is Achilles’ father, so ‘we’ means the gods. ἆ δειλώ is a dual vocative, ‘oh, you two miserable ones’ (the table’s ‘miserable’), τί … δόμεν is ‘why (did we) give’, an aorist infinitive in a question, and σφῶϊ is ‘you two’; Πηλῆϊ ἄνακτι is ‘to lord Peleus’ and θνητῷ ‘a mortal’. ὑμεῖς δ’ ἐστόν is ‘but you two are’, with the duals ἀγήρω ‘ageless’ and ἀθανάτω ‘immortal’ (the table’s ‘ageless and immortal’).

sentences.t: ἦ ἵνα δυστήνοισι μετ’ ἀνδράσιν ἄλγε’ ἔχητον;
sentences.l: Was it so that among wretched men you two might be beset by pains?
sentences.i: Was it so that you two might be beset by pains among wretched men?
sentences.n: A second question in the same speech. ἦ ἵνα is ‘was it so that’, and ἔχητον is a dual subjunctive of ἔχω; ἄλγε’ ἔχητον is ‘you two might be beset by pains’ (the table’s ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα ‘beset by pains’); δυστήνοισι is the table’s ‘wretched’ and μετ’ ἀνδράσιν ‘among men’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τί πού ἐστιν ὀϊζυρώτερον ἀνδρὸς
πάντων, ὅσσά τε γαῖαν ἔπι πνείει τε καὶ ἕρπει.
sentences.l:
For indeed not anything anywhere is more sorrowful than man
of all, as many as upon the earth breathe and creep.
sentences.i: For surely there is nothing anywhere more sorrowful than man, of all the things that breathe and creep upon the earth.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ is ‘for indeed not’, τί πού ‘anything anywhere’, and ὀϊζυρώτερον ἀνδρός is ‘more sorrowful than man’, a comparative with the genitive of comparison (the table’s ὀϊζυρός ‘sorrowful’); πάντων is ‘of all’, with ὅσσα … πνείει τε καὶ ἕρπει ‘as many as breathe and creep’, the singular verb with the neuter plural subject. γαῖαν ἔπι is ‘upon the earth’ (ἔπι after its noun).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ μὰν ὑμῖν γε καὶ ἅρμασι δαιδαλέοισιν
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης ἐποχήσεται·
sentences.l:
But indeed not upon you and the finely wrought chariot
will Hector, Priam’s son, be carried;
sentences.i: But Hector, son of Priam, shall not ride upon you two and the finely wrought chariot;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ μάν is ‘but truly not’, and ὑμῖν … καὶ ἅρμασι δαιδαλέοισιν is a dative ‘upon you and the finely wrought chariot’ (ὑμῖν is a plural form, not the dual σφῶϊν, but the two horses are meant, and the English says ‘you two’) (the table’s δαιδαλέος ‘finely wrought’, with the plural ἅρμασι used of one chariot). ἐποχήσεται is a future middle of ἐποχέομαι ‘ride upon, be carried upon’, and Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης is ‘Hector, son of Priam’.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἐάσω.
sentences.l: for I will not allow it.
sentences.i: for I will not allow it.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ is ‘for … not’, and ἐάσω is the future of ἐάω ‘allow’; the object is left out, ‘it’, that Hector should ride on them.

sentences.t: ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ὡς καὶ τεύχε’ ἔχει καὶ ἐπεύχεται αὔτως;
sentences.l: Is it not enough that he both has the armour and vaunts just so?
sentences.i: Is it not enough that he has the armour and cries out in triumph to no purpose?
sentences.n: The armour is Achilles’, which Hector took from Patroclus’ body. ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ὡς is ‘is it not enough that’, τεύχε’ ἔχει is ‘has the armour’, and ἐπεύχεται is ‘cries out in triumph’ (the table’s Iliad sense, 5.119). αὔτως is ‘just so’ in the literal and ‘to no purpose’ in the English (the table’s pair, 2.342); it could also be read ‘merely’, and the Greek does not settle whether Zeus means that the boasting is idle or that it is only boasting.

sentences.t:
σφῶϊν δ’ ἐν γούνεσσι βαλῶ μένος ἠδ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
ὄφρα καὶ Αὐτομέδοντα σαώσετον ἐκ πολέμοιο
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς·
sentences.i: And I will cast might into your knees and into your hearts, so that you two may save Automedon too out of the war, to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: σφῶϊν is ‘to you two’; ἐν γούνεσσι … ἠδ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ is ‘in the knees … and in the heart’, and βαλῶ is the future ‘I will cast’; μένος is ‘might’ (the table’s word, 2.387). ὄφρα … σαώσετον is a dual aorist subjunctive of σαόω ‘save’, ‘so that you two may save’, with καὶ Αὐτομέδοντα ‘Automedon too’ and ἐκ πολέμοιο νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς ‘out of the war to the hollow ships’.

sentences.t:
ἔτι γάρ σφισι κῦδος ὀρέξω
κτείνειν, εἰς ὅ κε νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἀφίκωνται
δύῃ τ’ ἠέλιος καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἱερὸν ἔλθῃ·
sentences.l:
for still to them glory I will grant
to kill, until they reach the well-benched ships
and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on.”
sentences.i: for I will still grant them glory in killing, until they reach the well-benched ships and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on.”
sentences.n: σφισι ‘to them’ is the Trojans, who are not named in the speech; the ships are the Achaean ships. ἔτι γάρ is ‘for still’, κῦδος ὀρέξω is ‘I will grant glory’ (the table’s ὀρέξῃ ‘grant glory’, 5.33; the verb is literally ‘stretch out’), and κτείνειν is ‘to kill’. εἰς ὅ κε … ἀφίκωνται is ‘until they reach’ (a subjunctive plural; the same words stand in the singular in a published part of the Iliad), with νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ‘the well-benched ships’; the last line, δύῃ τ’ ἠέλιος καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἱερὸν ἔλθῃ, is the table’s ‘and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on’ (the table’s row for 11.194). The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἵπποισιν ἐνέπνευσεν μένος ἠΰ.
sentences.l: So having spoken, to the horses he breathed in good might.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and breathed good might into the horses.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, and ἐνέπνευσεν is an aorist ‘breathed into’; ἵπποισιν is ‘into the horses’ (dative). ἠΰ is the neuter of ἠΰς, ‘good, noble’, agreeing with μένος ‘might’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἀπὸ χαιτάων κονίην οὖδας δὲ βαλόντε
ῥίμφα φέρον θοὸν ἅρμα μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
and the two, from their manes the dust to the ground
having thrown, nimbly carried the swift chariot among Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.i: and the two, shaking the dust from their manes to the ground, carried the swift chariot nimbly among the Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.n: τὼ is the two horses. ἀπὸ … βαλόντε is a dual aorist participle, ‘having thrown off’, with κονίην ‘dust’, χαιτάων ‘from the manes’ (epic -άων) and οὖδας δέ ‘to the ground’ (-δε of direction); φέρον is the imperfect ‘carried’, ῥίμφα the table’s ‘nimbly’, and θοὸν ἅρμα ‘the swift chariot’. μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς is ‘among the Trojans and Achaeans’, into the fighting between them.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Αὐτομέδων μάχετ’ ἀχνύμενός περ ἑταίρου
ἵπποις ἀΐσσων ὥς τ’ αἰγυπιὸς μετὰ χῆνας·
sentences.l:
and against them Automedon fought, though grieving for his companion,
darting with the horses like a vulture among geese;
sentences.i: And Automedon fought against them, though he grieved for his companion, darting with his horses like a vulture among geese;
sentences.n: τοῖσι is ‘them’, the men the horses have been carried among, and ἐπ’ with the dative is ‘against’; Αὐτομέδων is Automedon, who fights from the chariot. ἀχνύμενος is the table’s ‘grieving’, and ἑταίρου ‘for his companion’ is Patroclus; περ gives ‘although’. ἵπποις ἀΐσσων is ‘darting with the horses’ (the table’s ‘dart’), and αἰγυπιός is a large bird of prey, ‘vulture’, the usual rendering, μετὰ χῆνας ‘among geese’.

sentences.t:
ῥέα μὲν γὰρ φεύγεσκεν ὑπ’ ἐκ Τρώων ὀρυμαγδοῦ,
ῥεῖα δ’ ἐπαΐξασκε πολὺν καθ’ ὅμιλον ὀπάζων.
sentences.l:
for easily he would flee from beneath, out of the din of the Trojans,
and easily he would rush on through the great throng, pressing on;
sentences.i: for he would easily escape from the din of the Trojans, and easily rush on through the great throng, pressing on;
sentences.n: ῥέα and ῥεῖα are the same word, ‘easily’, said twice. φεύγεσκεν and ἐπαΐξασκε are iterative (-σκ-), ‘he would flee’ and ‘would rush on’. ὑπ’ ἐκ Τρώων ὀρυμαγδοῦ is ‘from under, out of, the Trojans’ din’ (the table’s ὀρυμαγδός ‘din’), and πολὺν καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘through the great throng’. ὀπάζων is the participle of ὀπάζω ‘make follow’, here ‘pressing on’; no object is given, and whether he presses the horses on or the enemy is not said.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐχ ᾕρει φῶτας ὅτε σεύαιτο διώκειν·
sentences.l: but he did not take men whenever he rushed to pursue;
sentences.i: but he did not catch men whenever he set off in pursuit;
sentences.n: ᾕρει is the imperfect of αἱρέω ‘take, catch’, with φῶτας ‘men’; ὅτε σεύαιτο is an optative of repeated action in the past, ‘whenever he rushed’, and διώκειν is ‘to pursue’. The point of the clause is that he could drive in and out of the Trojans but could not kill them.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πως ἦν οἶον ἐόνθ’ ἱερῷ ἐνὶ δίφρῳ
ἔγχει ἐφορμᾶσθαι καὶ ἐπίσχειν ὠκέας ἵππους.
sentences.l:
for in no way was it possible, being alone in the sacred chariot,
to attack with the spear and also to hold in the swift horses.
sentences.i: for it was in no way possible, being alone in the sacred chariot, to attack with the spear and also to hold in the swift horses.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πως ἦν is ‘for in no way was it possible’, and οἶον ἐόντ(α) is ‘being alone’ (a lone man in the car, accusative with the infinitives). ἱερῷ … δίφρῳ is ‘in the sacred chariot’, ἱερός being the usual ‘sacred’. ἐφορμᾶσθαι is ‘to attack’ (the middle of ἐφορμάω) with ἔγχει ‘with the spear’, and ἐπίσχειν is ‘to hold in, check’; ὠκέας ἵππους is ‘the swift horses’.

sentences.t:
ὀψὲ δὲ δή μιν ἑταῖρος ἀνὴρ ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
Ἀλκιμέδων υἱὸς Λαέρκεος Αἱμονίδαο·
sentences.l:
And at last a companion, a man, saw him with his eyes,
Alcimedon, son of Laerces, Haemon’s son;
sentences.i: And at last a companion saw him with his eyes, Alcimedon, son of Laerces, the son of Haemon;
sentences.n: ὀψὲ δὲ δή is ‘and at last’, and μιν ‘him’ is Automedon; ἑταῖρος ἀνήρ is ‘a companion, a man’, that is, a fellow-fighter, and ἴδεν is the unaugmented aorist ‘saw’. Ἀλκιμέδων is Alcimedon, a Myrmidon; Λαέρκεος is the uncontracted genitive ‘of Laerces’, and Αἱμονίδαο ‘Haemon’s son’ is a further patronymic agreeing with it.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὄπιθεν δίφροιο καὶ Αὐτομέδοντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and he stood behind the chariot and addressed Automedon:
sentences.i: He stood behind the chariot and spoke to Automedon:
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist ‘stood’, ὄπιθεν δίφροιο is ‘behind the chariot’, and προσηύδα ‘addressed’ is the imperfect; Αὐτομέδοντα is the accusative, the person addressed.

sentences.t:
Αὐτόμεδον, τίς τοί νυ θεῶν νηκερδέα βουλὴν
ἐν στήθεσσιν ἔθηκε, καὶ ἐξέλετο φρένας ἐσθλάς;
sentences.l:
“Automedon, which of the gods has put in your breast
a profitless plan, and taken away your good wits?
sentences.i: “Automedon, which of the gods has put a profitless plan in your breast, and taken away your good sense?
sentences.n: The speech is Alcimedon’s. τίς … θεῶν is ‘which of the gods’, and τοι is σοι ‘in your case’. νηκερδέα is ‘profitless’, from a negative prefix and κέρδος ‘gain’, and βουλήν is ‘plan’; ἐν στήθεσσιν ἔθηκε is ‘put in your breast’, and ἐξέλετο is ‘took away’. φρένας ἐσθλάς is the table’s ‘good wits, good sense’. The question is one question with two verbs.

sentences.t:
οἷον πρὸς Τρῶας μάχεαι πρώτῳ ἐν ὁμίλῳ
μοῦνος· ἀτάρ τοι ἑταῖρος ἀπέκτατο, τεύχεα δ’ Ἕκτωρ
αὐτὸς ἔχων ὤμοισιν ἀγάλλεται Αἰακίδαο.
sentences.l:
How you fight against the Trojans in the foremost throng
alone! But your companion has been killed, and the armour Hector
himself, having it on his shoulders, exults, of the descendant of Aeacus.”
sentences.i: How you fight against the Trojans in the foremost throng, alone! Your companion has been killed, and Hector himself, wearing on his shoulders the armour of the descendant of Aeacus, exults in it.”
sentences.n: οἷον is the exclamatory ‘how’, with μάχεαι ‘you fight’ (the uncontracted epic second person singular, Attic μάχῃ); πρώτῳ ἐν ὁμίλῳ is ‘in the foremost throng’ and μοῦνος ‘alone’. ἀτάρ is ‘but’, τοι is σοι ‘your’, and ἀπέκτατο is an aorist in middle form with passive sense, ‘was killed’, said of Patroclus. τεύχεα … Αἰακίδαο is ‘the armour of the descendant of Aeacus’, Achilles’; αὐτὸς ἔχων ὤμοισιν is ‘himself wearing it on his shoulders’, and ἀγάλλεται is ‘exults’ and has no object of its own: τεύχεα is the object of ἔχων, set first for emphasis (the English adds ‘in it’ for the English).

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Αὐτομέδων προσέφη Διώρεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Automedon, Diores’ son:
sentences.i: Then Automedon, son of Diores, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: τὸν is ‘him’, Alcimedon, δ’ αὖτ’ ‘then in turn’, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’; Διώρεος υἱός is ‘Diores’ son’. The pattern is the table’s τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός.

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίμεδον τίς γάρ τοι Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλος ὁμοῖος
ἵππων ἀθανάτων ἐχέμεν δμῆσίν τε μένος τε,
εἰ μὴ Πάτροκλος θεόφιν μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος
ζωὸς ἐών;
sentences.l:
“Alcimedon, for who of the Achaeans other is like you
to hold of immortal horses both the mastering and the might,
if not Patroclus, a counsellor, the equal of gods,
while he lived?
sentences.i: “Alcimedon, for what other Achaean is your equal in holding the immortal horses, with mastery of them and might, if not Patroclus, the counsellor equal to the gods, while he lived?
sentences.n: Ἀλκίμεδον is the vocative of the same man (the name is Ἀλκιμέδων in 467). τίς … ἄλλος ὁμοῖος is ‘who else is like’, with the infinitive ἐχέμεν ‘to hold’, and ἵππων ἀθανάτων ‘immortal horses’ its object; δμῆσίν τε μένος τε is two nouns, ‘mastering’ (δμῆσις, ‘taming, subduing’) and ‘might’, as what the holding takes, and how they hang on ἐχέμεν is not fully certain. εἰ μὴ Πάτροκλος is ‘if not Patroclus’; μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος is ‘a counsellor, an equal’ (the table’s ‘counsellor’ and ἀτάλαντος ‘equal’), with θεόφιν ‘to the gods’, the ending -φιν marking no number, as in the table. ζωὸς ἐών is ‘while he was alive’.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖ θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κιχάνει.
sentences.l: now in turn death and fate overtake him.
sentences.i: Now, in turn, death and fate overtake him.
sentences.n: νῦν αὖ is ‘now in turn’, the contrast with ‘while he lived’; θάνατος is ‘death’ and μοῖρα ‘fate’, and κιχάνει is ‘overtakes, reaches’, with Patroclus as the unspoken object.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα
δέξαι, ἐγὼ δ’ ἵππων ἀποβήσομαι, ὄφρα μάχωμαι.
sentences.l:
But you, for your part, the whip and the glossy reins
take, and I from the horses will step down, so that I may fight.”
sentences.i: But you, for your part, take the whip and the glossy reins, and I will step down from the horses so that I may fight.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σὺ μέν is ‘but you, for your part’, and μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα is ‘the whip and the glossy reins’ (the table’s σιγαλόεις ‘glossy’). δέξαι is an aorist imperative middle of δέχομαι, ‘take’; ἀποβήσομαι is the future ‘I will step down’, with ἵππων ‘from the horses’ (genitive of separation). ὄφρα μάχωμαι is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may fight’. The speech ends here.
